The Yucatan deer mouse (Peromyscus yucatanicus) is a small cricetid rodent endemic to the Yucatan Peninsula, where it inhabits tropical dry forests and scrublands. Field studies report that neonatal pups emerge from the birth canal weighing approximately 2.6 grams [Wwb = approximately 2.6 grams], a modest mass that reflects the altricial state typical of many peromyscines. These pups, entirely dependent on maternal milk, begin suckling immediately after parturition and remain housed in well-concealed nests constructed of dried vegetation. Growth proceeds steadily through the early postnatal period, with the eyes opening around ten days after parturition and the first solid foods being explored shortly thereafter. Under the warm thermal conditions of the region, which correspond to a core body temperature of approximately 36.6 °C [T = 36.6 °C], the transition from exclusive milk ingestion to nutritional independence from maternal care concludes quite rapidly; weaning, defined as the cessation of lactation and the onset of a fully solid-food diet, occurs at roughly 22 days after birth [tx = roughly 22 days after birth]. This relatively abbreviated nursing interval is consistent with patterns observed in other heteromyid and murid rodents inhabiting seasonally resource-poor environments.

Reproductive timing in Peromyscus yucatanicus follows a predictable schedule under controlled laboratory conditions. Gestation, from the moment of internal fertilisation through to live birth, lasts for a period of 30 days [tg = 30 days] when females are maintained at a stable core temperature of 36.6 °C [T = 36.6 °C]. This duration aligns closely with the gestational intervals documented for several other members of the Peromyscus genus and suggests a relatively standard placental developmental trajectory. Following the birth event, the altricial neonates undergo a period of rapid somatic growth and physiological maturation. The onset of reproductive capability in females, marking the conclusion of the juvenile stage and the beginning of active gametogenesis, occurs after a post-natal interval of 51.5 days after birth [tp = 51.5 days after birth], again assessed under the same thermoneutral conditions of 36.6 °C at a temperature of 36.6 °C [T = 36.6 °C]. This developmental milestone, which corresponds to the first oestrus and ovulation event, enables young females to begin contributing to the population within their first few months of life, a life-history strategy that enhances the species' capacity for rapid population turnover in fluctuating tropical habitats.

The maximum reproductive output of the Yucatan deer mouse illustrates the strong fecundity potential that offsets its modest adult body size. Litter sizes range from just one to as many as seven pups per parturition event [N_R_i = seven pups per parturition event], a broad range that reflects plasticity in response to resource availability and maternal condition. In concert with this variability in per-litter output, breeding females in the wild are capable of producing multiple litters across the annual cycle. Available data indicate that the maximum observed rate of parturition events is approximately 3.7 litters per year [F_R_i = approximately 3.7 litters per year], a frequency sustained only under optimal nutritional and thermal conditions, specifically at a core body temperature of 36.6 °C [T = 36.6 °C]. This combined expression of a broad litter-size range and a moderate annual birthing frequency generates considerable overall reproductive potential, enabling populations to rebound swiftly after periods of environmental stress or high predation pressure imposed by snakes and raptorial birds endemic to the Yucatan landscape.

Adult body size in Peromyscus yucatanicus reaches a definitive maximum at the conclusion of the growth phase, after which individuals are considered fully grown. The ultimate wet weight, or asymptotic adult body mass, attained by reproductively mature individuals in stable captive populations is approximately 35 grams [Wwi = approximately 35 grams]. This body size places the species among the larger members of the Peromyscus leucopus species group, a finding consistent with the relatively productive tropical habitats it occupies. Males and females show only modest sexual size dimorphism, though lactating females may temporarily achieve slightly elevated masses due to mammary tissue hypertrophy and increased fluid retention. Comparative data from related forms, such as Peromyscus maniculatus, reveal that the 35-gram asymptotic mass reflects a life-history strategy oriented toward moderate longevity and iterative breeding rather than toward an extreme semelparous investment. The mature body mass is achieved several months after weaning, with growth decelerating notably after the onset of puberty and the initiation of reproductive activity.

Lifespan in the Yucatan deer mouse, when measured under conditions that minimise extrinsic mortality sources such as predation and food scarcity, provides insight into the species' intrinsic physiological limits. Captive individuals, housed at a core body temperature of 36.6 °C [T = 36.6 °C], have been documented to survive for a maximum of 548 days [am = 548 days], which corresponds to roughly one and a half years. This longevity is relatively brief compared to some temperate-dwelling peromyscines, a pattern that may be linked to the elevated metabolic costs incurred by a continuously warm-adapted physiology. In the wild, most individuals are unlikely to reach this extreme age, with field data indicating that average adult survivorship is substantially lower due to predation by small carnivores and owls. Nonetheless, the documented captive maximum underscores that the species' pace of life is rapid, with accelerated maturation, high fecundity, and a compressed reproductive window consistent with a strategy that maximises short-term population growth in a climatically stable but predator-rich environment.
